title: Docker
subtitle: CONTAINERS 101
description: Docker is the standard for building, shipping, and running containers. Learn images, containers, volumes, networking, and Compose.

Docker.desc: Docker is an open platform for developing, shipping, and running applications inside containers. It separates your app from your infrastructure so you can deliver software quickly.
Docker.pricing: Docker Desktop: free for personal use, $21/mo teams
Docker.variants: Docker Desktop • Docker Engine • Docker Hub • Docker Compose
Docker.devNote: Learn the image → container lifecycle first. Everything else builds on that.
Docker.learn: Docker is a shipping container for software. Your app + its dependencies go in the box. The box runs the same everywhere.

Core Concepts.desc: The fundamental building blocks of Docker: images, containers, Dockerfile, and the registry.
Core Concepts.devNote: Master docker build, run, ps, logs, exec before anything else.

Image.desc: A Docker image is a read-only template with instructions for creating a container. Built from a Dockerfile, layered for efficiency.
Image.devNote: Use multi-stage builds to keep final images small. Never put secrets in images.
Image.learn: An image is a recipe. A container is the meal cooked from that recipe. You can cook many meals from one recipe.

Container.desc: A runnable instance of an image. Isolated process with its own filesystem, network, and process space. Ephemeral by default.
Container.devNote: Containers are ephemeral — data written inside is lost on removal. Use volumes for persistence.
Container.learn: A container is a running image. Like a VM but lighter — shares the host OS kernel, starts in milliseconds.

Dockerfile.desc: A text file with instructions to build a Docker image. Each instruction creates a layer. FROM, RUN, COPY, CMD, EXPOSE are the key directives.
Dockerfile.devNote: Order matters for layer caching. Put COPY package.json before COPY . to cache npm install.
Dockerfile.learn: A Dockerfile is a recipe card. Each line is a step. Docker executes them top to bottom and caches each layer.

Docker Hub.desc: The default public registry for Docker images. Pull official images (nginx, postgres, node) or push your own.
Docker Hub.pricing: Free for public repos, $5/mo for private
Docker Hub.variants: Docker Hub • GitHub Container Registry • AWS ECR • GCR
Docker Hub.devNote: Use specific tags (node:20-alpine) not latest in production. Latest can break builds.
Docker Hub.learn: Docker Hub is the App Store for container images. Pull nginx in one command: docker pull nginx.

Networking.desc: How containers communicate with each other and the outside world. Bridge, host, overlay, and none network drivers.
Networking.devNote: Use custom bridge networks — containers on the same network resolve each other by name.

Bridge Network.desc: Default network driver. Creates a private internal network on the host. Containers on the same bridge can communicate by container name.
Bridge Network.devNote: Always create user-defined bridge networks — the default bridge doesn't support DNS resolution by name.
Bridge Network.learn: A bridge network is a virtual switch inside your machine. Containers plug into it and talk to each other.

Port Mapping.desc: Map a container port to a host port with -p hostPort:containerPort. Makes the container service accessible from outside.
Port Mapping.devNote: Use 127.0.0.1:8080:80 to bind only to localhost, not all interfaces — safer for dev.
Port Mapping.learn: Port mapping is a doorbell. -p 8080:80 means: ring the doorbell on 8080, it rings inside the container on 80.

Overlay Network.desc: Connects multiple Docker daemons across hosts. Used in Docker Swarm for multi-host container communication.
Overlay Network.devNote: Overlay networks require Swarm mode. For Kubernetes, use CNI plugins instead.

Host Network.desc: Container shares the host's network stack directly. No network isolation. Best performance but no port mapping needed.
Host Network.devNote: Host network only works on Linux. On Mac/Windows Docker Desktop, it behaves differently.

Storage.desc: Persist data beyond container lifecycle. Volumes, bind mounts, and tmpfs are the three storage options.
Storage.devNote: Prefer named volumes over bind mounts for portability. Bind mounts are great for dev hot-reload.

Volumes.desc: Managed by Docker, stored in /var/lib/docker/volumes. Best for persistent data. Can be shared between containers and backed up easily.
Volumes.variants: Named volumes • Anonymous volumes • Volume plugins (AWS EFS, etc.)
Volumes.devNote: Use named volumes in production. docker volume ls and docker volume inspect are your friends.
Volumes.learn: A volume is a USB drive managed by Docker. Plug it into any container. Data survives container removal.

Bind Mounts.desc: Mount a host directory or file into a container. Changes on host reflect immediately in container. Perfect for development.
Bind Mounts.devNote: Bind mounts depend on host directory structure — not portable. Use volumes for production.
Bind Mounts.learn: A bind mount is a window into your host filesystem. The container sees your files live — edit on host, see changes in container instantly.

tmpfs.desc: In-memory temporary filesystem. Data is never written to disk. Useful for sensitive data or high-speed temporary storage.
tmpfs.devNote: tmpfs data is lost when container stops. Never use for data you need to keep.

Orchestration.desc: Run and manage multiple containers together. Docker Compose for local multi-container apps, Swarm for production clusters.
Orchestration.devNote: Use Compose for dev. For production at scale, Kubernetes is the industry standard.

Docker Compose.desc: Define and run multi-container applications with a YAML file. One command to start your entire stack: docker compose up.
useCases: Local dev with app + DB + cache
Docker Compose.devNote: Use depends_on with healthcheck condition to ensure services start in order. Use .env files for environment variables.
Docker Compose.learn: Compose is a conductor's score. It tells Docker: start these containers, connect them on this network, mount these volumes — all from one YAML file.

Docker Swarm.desc: Native Docker clustering and orchestration. Turn multiple Docker hosts into a single virtual host. Simpler than Kubernetes.
Docker Swarm.variants: Manager nodes • Worker nodes • Global services • Replicated services
Docker Swarm.devNote: Swarm is simpler than Kubernetes but less feature-rich. Good for small teams who don't need the full K8s ecosystem.
Docker Swarm.learn: Swarm turns many Docker hosts into one. You deploy a service, Swarm decides which node runs it and keeps it running.
